label: AQ 0021
title: The refiners that ran out of ideas

questions.q: Is a chain ever the right shape?
questions.a: Yes. In the MacNet study (Qian et al., ICLR 2025), no topology won every task: a chain suited software development and step-by-step logic problems, while denser meshes did better on average. Keep a chain when each step is a different job, like draft then format, not for the same job repeated.

teach.title: How it works: why the chain stalls, and what to change

questions.q: What if you can't test the output?
questions.a: Then picking becomes the weak spot. Large Language Monkeys found majority voting and reward models used to pick among samples plateau beyond several hundred samples. Use a judge comparing drafts side by side, swap their order since judges can favour one position, and add a human check where it matters.

questions.q: Why not just make the refiners argue?
questions.a: It helps. Du et al. (2023) had several agents debate and beat both a single agent and self-reflection on arithmetic and GSM8K. But on arithmetic, rounds past four added little, and agents that converged were not always right. Argument works best from different starting drafts or with real feedback.

questions.q: What does Self-Refine's code-optimisation curve look like across a first draft and three refinements?
questions.a: 22.0, 27.0, 27.9, 28.8: five points from the first refinement, then under one point each. The authors call it diminishing returns.

questions.q: Each independent draft has a 20% chance of the right approach. Roughly how likely is at least one of five to have it?
questions.a: About 67%: all five miss with chance 0.8 to the power 5, about 0.33. That assumes the drafts really are independent, and you still need tests or a judge to find the good one.
